queries.hook: I feel like an imposter. Inside, my mind won't settle, and I don't know how to carry it.
queries.diagnose: Guilt and shame turn the mind against itself; the one who keeps pushing themselves down becomes their own enemy.
queries.steady: A mistake is something you did, not who you are; no one who tries to do good is ever lost.
queries.act: Be on your own side: lift yourself up, make amends where you can, and begin again; no one who does good is lost.

hook.speaker: Tulsidas
hook.setting: Bharat walks toward Ram, slowed by shame, quickened by love.
hook.sanskrit: फेरति मनहुँ मातु कृत खोरी। चलत भगति बल धीरज धोरी॥ जब समुझत रघुनाथ सुभाऊ। तब पथ परत उताइल पाऊ ॥
hook.line: Shame slowed him. But whenever he remembered Ram's nature, his feet moved faster.
hook.translation: It was as if his mother's wrong held him back, while the strength of devotion drove him on like a patient ox. Whenever he remembered Raghunath's nature, his feet moved faster on the path.
hook.for_you: Your mind won't settle while you are working, and a verse was chosen with that weight in mind.
hook.first_line: Your mind won't settle while you are working, and a verse was chosen with that weight in mind.

alternates.speaker: Vibhishan
alternates.setting: Vibhishan, Ravana's good-hearted brother, describes his life in Ravana's court.
alternates.sanskrit: सुनहु पवनसुत रहनि हमारी। जिमि दसनन्हि महुँ जीभ बिचारी॥ तात कबहुँ मोहि जानि अनाथा। करिहहिं कृपा भानुकुल नाथा ॥
alternates.line: I live here like the tongue among the teeth.
alternates.translation: Son of the wind, hear how I live: like the poor tongue among the teeth. Friend, knowing me to be without support, will the Lord of the Sun dynasty ever show me grace?
alternates.why: Even in a hostile place there may be one ally; find them.

prasang.title: Hanuman finds a friend in Lanka
prasang.summary: Searching Lanka, Hanuman is surprised to find a house with Ram's name on it. Its owner, Vibhishan, Ravana's brother, says he lives in Lanka like a tongue among teeth. Hanuman tells him even a restless monkey like himself was given Ram's love.
prasang.story_hook: In a city of demons, Hanuman heard someone wake up and say Ram's name.
prasang.lesson: Even in a hostile place there may be one ally; find them.

alternates.speaker: Hanuman
alternates.setting: Having searched every house, garden and street of Lanka without finding Sita, Hanuman sits on the city wall and weighs what to do next.
alternates.line: What will Sugriva and the other monkeys say when I get back to Kishkindha?
alternates.translation: Or what will Sugriva say, and the assembled monkeys, and the two sons of Dasaratha, when I return to Kishkindha?
alternates.why: When you have looked everywhere, look again; giving up costs too much.

prasang.title: Hanuman's search and near despair
prasang.summary: Hanuman searches Lanka all night without finding Sita. He is close to despair, weighing what failure will mean for everyone, then tells himself that refusing to lose heart is the root of success, and searches again.
prasang.story_hook: Hanuman had searched every palace in Lanka by moonlight, and she was nowhere.
prasang.lesson: When you have looked everywhere, look again; giving up costs too much.

verse.speaker: Kakbhushundi
verse.setting: Kakbhushundi continues listing the diseases of the mind.
verse.sanskrit: ममता दादु कंडु इरषाई। हरष बिषाद गरह बहुताई॥ पर सुख देखि जरनि सोइ छई। कुष्ट दुष्टता मन कुटिलई ॥
verse.line: Envy is an itch. Burning at another's happiness is a wasting disease of the mind.
verse.translation: Possessiveness is ringworm and envy is the itch; the swings of elation and dejection are throat ailments. The burning you feel at another's happiness is consumption, and malice and a crooked mind are leprosy.
verse.why: Know your mind's diseases by name: confusion, anger, greed, envy, ego.

prasang.title: Garuda's seven questions
prasang.summary: Garuda asks seven questions: the rarest body, the greatest sorrow and joy, the nature of good and wicked people, the highest virtue and the worst wrong, and the diseases of the mind. Kakbhushundi answers: no sorrow like want, no joy like meeting good people; non-harm is highest and slander worst; delusion is the root disease, with lust, greed, anger, envy and ego as its symptoms.
prasang.lesson: Know your mind's diseases by name: confusion, anger, greed, envy, ego.

why: The illnesses of the mind (Ramcharitmanas, Uttar Kand 121-122 (Gita Press))
burning at another's joy is named as an illness one suffers, which can be treated

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.setting: From the section praising learning, addressed to proud rulers.
verse.sanskrit: हर्तुर्याति न गोचरं किमपि शं पुष्णाति यत् सर्वदा- ऽप्यर्थिभ्यः प्रतिपाद्यमानमनिशं प्राप्नोति वृद्धिं पराम् । कल्पान्तेष्वपि न प्रयाति निधनं विद्याख्यमन्तर्धनं येषां तान् प्रति मानमुज्झत नृपाः कस्तैः सह स्पर्धते ॥
verse.line: Learning is wealth no thief can see. It grows when you give it away and never perishes.
verse.translation: It never comes within a thief's sight; it always nourishes some deep good; given to those who ask, it grows greater; even at the end of an age it does not perish. Kings, drop your pride before those who own this inner wealth called learning. Who can compete with them?
verse.why: What you learn and how you speak are the wealth no one can take from you.

prasang.title: Nitishatakam: In praise of learning and the learned
prasang.summary: Bhartrihari praises learning as wealth no thief can take and speech as the one lasting ornament, then turns to good company and the three kinds of people who face obstacles. It ends with the 'sword's-edge vow' of the good.
prasang.lesson: What you learn and how you speak are the wealth no one can take from you.

why: What one has learned cannot be taken
A wealth the rich do not outrank

verse.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse.setting: From the section on wealth: on keeping your dignity before the rich.
verse.sanskrit: यद्धात्रा निजभालपट्टलिखितं स्तोकं महद्वा धनं तत् प्राप्नोति मरुस्थलेऽपि नितरां मेरौ ततो नाधिकम् । तद्धीरो भव वित्तवत्सु कृपणां वृत्तिं वृथा मा कृथाः कूपे पश्य पयोनिधावपि घटो गृह्णाति तुल्यं जलम् ॥
verse.line: A pot draws the same water from a well or the ocean. Keep your dignity before the rich.
verse.translation: Whatever wealth, small or great, the Creator has written on your forehead, you will get it even in a desert, and no more even on Mount Meru. So be steady; do not play the beggar before the rich for nothing. Look: a pot draws the same water from a well as from the ocean.
verse.why: Money changes how others see you, not who you are. Give it, enjoy it, or lose it.
verse.misuse: Not a reason to stop working or asking for fair pay; a reason not to grovel.

prasang.title: Nitishatakam: On wealth
prasang.summary: A wry look at money: how the world flatters the rich and forgets the broke, wealth's three destinies, and how distance and neglect ruin what we value. It closes with advice to the chataka bird not to plead before every cloud.
prasang.lesson: Money changes how others see you, not who you are. Give it, enjoy it, or lose it.

why: No need to demean oneself before the rich

verse.speaker: Kalakavrikshiya
verse.setting: The sage to the ruined prince Kshemadarshi, who keeps longing for what he lost.
verse.line: Want what is within reach. Enjoy what is here now. Don't grieve over what hasn't happened.
verse.translation: Wish for what can be had, never for what cannot. Enjoy what is in front of you now, and do not grieve over what has not yet come.
verse.why: Grief can't restore what's gone. Want what's within reach, and let others' success be.

prasang.title: Kalakavrikshiya consoles the fallen prince
prasang.summary: Prince Kshemadarshi has lost his kingdom and wealth. The sage Kalakavrikshiya tells him grief has no power to restore what is gone, to want what is within reach, and to make peace with others' good fortune.
prasang.lesson: Grief can't restore what's gone. Want what's within reach, and let others' success be.

why: Enjoying what is present is named as the practice
plan_v3.writer_note: Letting-go teaching for a reader who is building something. Explain it through their own situation and feeling: what is released is the grip that hurts them, never their love, their hope or their work. Never say or imply 'stop caring' or 'your hope is the problem'. Read it after the guard verse, which reassures first.

guard.line: A pot draws the same water from a well or the ocean. Keep your dignity before the rich.

verse.speaker: Vasishtha
verse.setting: A powerful king offers a fortune for the sage's cow, the source of his whole way of life.
verse.sanskrit: नाहं शतसहस्रेण नापि कोटिशतैर्गवाम्॥ राजन् दास्यामि शबलां राशिभी रजतस्य वा। न परित्यागमयं मत्सकाशादरिंदम ॥
verse.line: Not for any price. Some things are not for sale, however powerful the buyer.
verse.translation: Not for a hundred thousand cows, not for a billion, not for heaps of silver, O king, will I give up Shabala. She stays with me.
verse.why: Envy and force cannot take what someone will not give; real power is built inside.

prasang.title: The king who wanted the cow
prasang.summary: King Vishvamitra is feasted by the sage Vasishtha and covets the wish-granting cow that made it possible. Vasishtha refuses every offer; the king takes her by force and is routed, then fails again with divine weapons. Humbled, he resolves to transform himself through inner discipline instead of force.
prasang.story_hook: A king who had everything saw one thing he could not buy, and it undid him.
prasang.lesson: Envy and force cannot take what someone will not give; real power is built inside.

why: what sustains his life is not for sale
a plain no to someone far more powerful

story.title: 'Sisters and Brothers of America': Chicago, 11 September 1893
characters: Delegates and audience of the World's Parliament of Religions
story.story_hook: On 11 September 1893, a young Indian monk with no formal invitation stood up in Chicago and said five words that brought the hall to its feet.
story.summary: An unknown 30-year-old monk from India, with no invitation and little money, rises on the Parliament's opening day and greets the hall as 'Sisters and Brothers of America'. The audience stands and applauds for minutes. In a five-minute address he says India's faith accepts all religions as true and hopes the day marks the death-knell of fanaticism.
story.lesson: You can belong fully to your own tradition and still honour every other path.
story.hook_title: Vivekananda had no invitation, and five words brought Chicago to its feet
story.teaser: Vivekananda had no invitation, and five words brought Chicago to its feet
